title: Morton et al. 2018 - Protein supplementation meta-analysis
text: Morton et al. pooled 49 resistance training studies and found that protein supplementation produced a small but meaningful improvement in fat-free mass and strength compared with training alone. The dose-response analysis suggested that gains leveled off around 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day, with the upper end of the confidence interval close to 2.2 grams per kilogram per day. For practical coaching, this supports a daily target around 1.6 to 2.2 g/kg for people trying to maximize hypertrophy, with higher intakes mainly useful when calories are low, the athlete is lean, or appetite and meal timing make it easier to overshoot slightly.

title: Schoenfeld and Aragon 2018 - Protein timing and meal distribution
text: Schoenfeld and Aragon reviewed the meal-level evidence for muscle protein synthesis and concluded that total daily protein intake remains the main driver of adaptation, but distribution still matters. Their practical target was roughly 0.4 grams of protein per kilogram per meal across at least four meals to cover the observed daily range that supports hypertrophy. The paper also emphasizes that many people can do well anywhere from about 0.25 to 0.4 g/kg per meal depending on body size, food quality, and total daily intake. The coaching takeaway is to hit daily protein first, then spread it across three to five meals rather than saving almost all of it for a single sitting.

title: Aragon and Schoenfeld 2013 - Nutrient timing position review
text: Aragon and Schoenfeld reviewed the evidence behind the so-called anabolic window and argued that the narrow thirty-minute deadline often repeated in gym culture is overstated. The most important factor is that protein is consumed within a broader peri-workout period, especially when pre-training meals were many hours earlier. Their review supports focusing on total daily protein, with pre- and post-training meals used to make the daily plan easier and to support recovery. This paper is useful when correcting rigid myths: athletes do not need to panic if they cannot eat immediately after a session, but they also should not ignore protein intake for the entire day.

title: Helms et al. 2014 - Natural bodybuilding contest preparation
text: Helms and colleagues summarized evidence-based strategies for lean athletes dieting to very low body fat. The recommendations favored slower weight-loss rates, high protein intake, resistance training maintenance, and moderation rather than extreme restriction. Protein recommendations were notably higher during energy restriction, roughly 2.3 to 3.1 grams per kilogram of fat-free mass per day, because leaner athletes in harder cuts face a greater risk of muscle loss. The paper is a strong reminder that the deeper the deficit and the leaner the athlete, the more conservative the weekly rate of loss should become. In coaching terms, it supports small to moderate deficits, high protein, and performance preservation as the priority.

title: Schoenfeld et al. 2017 - Dose-response relationship for weekly resistance training volume
text: Schoenfeld and colleagues found a dose-response relationship between the number of weekly hard sets and hypertrophy. Programs performing ten or more sets per muscle group per week produced greater growth than lower-volume approaches in the aggregated data. The paper does not claim that more volume is always better without limit, but it strongly supports the idea that very low weekly volume usually leaves hypertrophy on the table once a lifter is past the beginner stage. A useful coaching interpretation is to start with recoverable volume, track performance and soreness, and then build toward a productive middle range rather than assuming one or two hard sets per week is enough.

title: Schoenfeld et al. 2016 - Training frequency meta-analysis
text: This meta-analysis compared resistance training frequencies and found that training a muscle group at least twice per week produced superior hypertrophy to once-weekly frequency when total volume was not tightly equated. The review helped popularize the practical rule that spreading work across the week often improves quality, recovery, and adherence. For coaching, the key idea is not that every athlete must use very high frequency, but that two or more exposures per week make it easier to accumulate effective volume, practice technique, and keep sessions from becoming excessively long or fatiguing.

title: Krieger 2010 - Single versus multiple sets meta-analysis
text: Krieger compared single-set and multiple-set resistance training protocols and found that multiple sets produced substantially greater hypertrophy than single-set programs. The gap was most relevant once the goal moved from general health to maximizing muscle growth. The study is frequently used to support the idea that a minimalist program can work, especially for beginners or busy periods, but that sustained hypertrophy usually benefits from more than one hard working set per exercise or muscle group. In programming conversations, this evidence supports moving past bare-minimum volume when progress stalls.

title: Thomas et al. 2016 - Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and ACSM position stand
text: The joint position stand from the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and the American College of Sports Medicine remains a practical foundation for sports nutrition. It supports carbohydrate targets that scale with training demand, protein amounts that support repair and adaptation, and hydration plans that match body size, climate, and sweat losses. The position stand is especially useful when a coach needs a broad evidence-backed framework rather than a niche optimization claim. For daily coaching, it supports aligning carbohydrate intake with workload, keeping fats sufficient for health, and treating hydration and electrolytes as performance variables rather than afterthoughts.

title: Trexler et al. 2014 - Metabolic adaptation to weight loss
text: Trexler and coauthors reviewed adaptive thermogenesis and the ways prolonged dieting reduces total energy expenditure beyond what body-mass changes alone would predict. Reductions in resting metabolic rate, spontaneous activity, and appetite-related hormones all contribute to plateaus and increased hunger. The key coaching implication is that a stalled cut does not automatically mean the athlete is noncompliant or broken. It often means energy expenditure has adapted. Practical responses include reassessing intake accuracy, increasing daily movement, reducing accumulated fatigue, and using planned maintenance periods or diet breaks when appropriate.

title: Kerksick et al. 2017 - International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand on nutrient timing
text: The ISSN position stand on nutrient timing concluded that timing strategies can matter, but mostly after the bigger rocks are in place: adequate daily energy, sufficient carbohydrate for training demands, and enough total protein. The paper discusses pre-session fueling, intra-session carbohydrate for longer or harder training, and post-session nutrition for recovery, while also making clear that timing is not a substitute for poor overall intake. In coaching practice, this means peri-workout advice should be individualized to session length, sport demands, and the athlete's tolerance, not treated as a universal ritual.

title: Watson 2015 - Recommended amount of sleep for healthy adults and athletes
text: Watson and collaborators summarized sleep recommendations and highlighted that athletes often need more sleep than the general minimum because heavy training, travel, and competition stress raise recovery demands. Seven to nine hours is a baseline target for healthy adults, but high-performing athletes may benefit from extending opportunity for sleep beyond that range. This source is useful because it grounds recovery advice in a broader health context rather than treating sleep as optional. In coaching, it supports checking sleep quality and quantity before making aggressive changes to training volume, intensity, or calorie intake.

title: Behm et al. 2016 - Acute effects of muscle stretching on performance
text: Behm and colleagues reviewed the short-term performance effects of stretching and found that prolonged static stretching before explosive or maximal tasks can reduce force and power output. The practical lesson is not that flexibility work is bad, but that long static holds are usually better placed after training or in separate mobility sessions. Before strength sessions, dynamic movements and progressive warm-up sets tend to prepare performance more effectively. This paper is most useful when a user asks whether to keep doing long passive stretches right before squats, sprints, or heavy compound lifts.
